name: Āyurveda
regions: Gandhāra and the north-west (tradition: Takṣaśilā; Pañcanada for Dṛḍhabala)
Tibet, Central Asia and Sri Lanka (transmissions)

tradition.text: beginningless (śāśvata, Ca Sū 30.27); revealed by Brahmā and brought to earth by Bharadvāja (Ca Sū 1) or by Dhanvantari as Divodāsa of Kāśī (Su Sū 1)

scholarly.text: classical compendia c. 2nd c. BCE – 7th c. CE; commentaries 9th–16th c.; living

transmissions_received.what: Atharvavedic healing and the self-description of Āyurveda as an upāṅga of the Atharvaveda (Su Sū 1.6; Ca Sū 30.21)
the principles and the three guṇas in the account of the person (Ca Śā 1.16-17, 1.63-66; Su Śā 1.3-9)
the six categories (sāmānya, viśeṣa, guṇa, dravya, karma, samavāya) as the foundations (Ca Sū 1.28-29, 1.44-52)

transmissions_given.what: the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya (translated into Tibetan, Tengyur) and its three-doṣa medicine, in the tradition's own later account received into the Four Tantras
shared three-humour doctrine and Sanskrit medical vocabulary (direction disputed)
doṣa vocabulary used for the purposes of the cleansing acts and breath retentions (HYP 2.21)
the frame of rasāyana and the pharmacological categories (rasa, guṇa, vīrya, vipāka) into which mercurial medicine was absorbed

distinctive_positions: Āyus (life) is the union of body, senses, mind and self; Āyurveda is the knowledge of what is wholesome and unwholesome, happy and unhappy life and its measure (Ca Sū 1.41-42).
Its purpose is twofold: protecting the health of the healthy and allaying the disorder of the sick (Ca Sū 30.26; Su Sū 1.14).
Health is the equilibrium (sāmya) of the dhātus, disease their disequilibrium (Ca Sū 9.4; AHS Sū 1.20).
The body has three doṣas (vāta, pitta, kapha); the mind has two (rajas and tamas) (Ca Sū 1.57; AHS Sū 1.21).
Three causes of all disease: wrong contact of senses and objects, failure of discernment (prajñāparādha), and time/transformation (pariṇāma) (Ca Sū 11.43).
Three kinds of therapy: resting on the divine (daiva-vyapāśraya), on reasoned application (yukti-vyapāśraya), and conquest of the mind (sattvāvajaya) (Ca Sū 11.54).
Four means of valid knowledge: authoritative testimony, perception, inference and yukti (Ca Sū 11.17).
Rebirth is established by all four means (Ca Sū 11.6-33); liberation (mokṣa) is the complete cessation of all feeling, attained through yoga and the recollection of truth (Ca Śā 1.137-155).
Āyurveda is beginningless and eternal; only its understanding and teaching have a beginning (Ca Sū 30.27).
It is a science of life, not itself a path of liberation: health is the root of dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣa (Ca Sū 1.15).
Like cures unlike: increase by the similar (sāmānya), decrease by the dissimilar (viśeṣa) (Ca Sū 1.44).
summary: The science of life (āyus), taught in the tradition's account by Brahmā and brought to earth through Indra — to Bharadvāja and Ātreya Punarvasu (the physicians' school) and to Dhanvantari as King Divodāsa of Kāśī (the surgeons' school). Its classical compendia (Caraka, Suśruta, Vāgbhaṭa) teach the three doṣas, seven dhātus and malas, the digestive fires, ojas and the channels; constitution; diet, daily and seasonal routine and good conduct; the eight branches; rejuvenation; and, in Caraka, a doctrine of the self, rebirth, yoga and liberation. It regards itself as eternal and as a limb of the Atharvaveda, and was practised across Vedic, Buddhist and Jain communities.
notes: family 'shared': the texts describe Āyurveda as an upaveda/upāṅga of the Atharvaveda (Su Sū 1.6; Ca Sū 30.21), but its authors and users include Buddhists (the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya's opening and its ten sinful acts; Ravigupta; the Bower manuscript) and Jains (Ugrāditya). Decision logged in REPORT.

name: The school of Ātreya (Ātreya-sampradāya, the physicians' line)
distinctive_positions: Primacy of internal medicine (kāyacikitsā).
Ātreya taught six disciples, each of whom composed a tantra; Agniveśa's was first (Ca Sū 1.30-33).
Surgical procedures are left to the Dhānvantarīyas (Ca Ci 5.44).
summary: The lineage of Punarvasu Ātreya and his six disciples (Agniveśa, Bhela, Jatūkarṇa, Parāśara, Hārīta, Kṣārapāṇi) whose tantras were approved by the assembly of sages (Ca Sū 1.30-40); Agniveśa's, redacted by Caraka and completed by Dṛḍhabala, survives as the Caraka Saṃhitā.
notes: 'Ātreya-sampradāya' is the later name for this line; the classical texts speak of Ātreya's disciples. Its separateness is now scholastic: all later Āyurveda draws on both schools.

name: The school of Dhanvantari (Dhānvantara-sampradāya, the surgeons' line)
distinctive_positions: Surgery (śalya) is the first and foremost of the eight limbs, being quick in effect and using instruments, knives, caustics and cautery (Su Sū 1.17-18).
The person treated is the union of the five elements with the embodied one (Su Sū 1.22).
Knowledge must be both textual and practical; the surgeon learns by practice on models (Su Sū 9).
summary: The lineage of Dhanvantari, born as King Divodāsa of Kāśī, who taught Suśruta and his fellow students with surgery as the root (Su Sū 1.3-21). Caraka names its specialists 'the Dhānvantarīyas' (Ca Ci 5.44, 5.63).

name: The Aṣṭavaidya physician families of Kerala
distinctive_positions: Hereditary transmission of the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya as the root text, learnt by heart.
Family lineages each master of the eight branches ('aṣṭa-vaidya').
summary: Hereditary Nampūtiri Brahmin physician families of Kerala who transmit Āyurveda through Vāgbhaṭa's Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya, with their own Malayalam and Sanskrit commentaries and treatment specialities.
notes: Names and number of the families, and their commentaries, not recorded here (uncertain); see REPORT gaps.

name: Rasa Śāstra (the science of mercury) and the Raseśvara-darśana
alt_names: Raseśvara-darśana (the philosophy of the Lord of rasa)

tradition.text: revealed by Bhairava (Śiva) to the Goddess (Rasārṇava); mercury is Śiva's own seed

scholarly.text: alchemical tantras c. 10th–13th c. CE; medical rasa compendia 13th–17th c.; still used in Āyurvedic pharmacy

transmissions_received.what: Śaiva tantric frame: initiation, mantra, liṅga worship, Bhairava and the Goddess as speakers

transmissions_given.what: mercurial and metallic medicines (bhasmas) absorbed into later Āyurvedic compendia (Śārṅgadhara, Bhāvaprakāśa)
the parallel of mercury and breath/mind (Rasārṇava 1.18-19; HYP 4.26-27)

distinctive_positions: Liberation in life (jīvanmukti) requires a stable, undecaying body; liberation promised only after the body falls cannot be seen and is 'meaningless' (Rasārṇava 1.8-13; SDS Raseśvara 4-5).
Mercury (pārada, 'that which carries across to the far shore of saṃsāra') is Śiva's seed; mica (abhraka) the Goddess's; their union yields the divine body (SDS Raseśvara 1-10).
The discipline of action (karmayoga) that stabilizes the body is twofold: mercury and breath (Rasārṇava 1.18-19).
Knowledge liberates; knowledge comes from practice; practice needs a stable body (Rasahṛdaya 1.10).
The goal of mercury is the body (dehavedha) and through it liberation, not the making of gold (SDS Raseśvara 23-25).
Mercury with its impurities is poison; only purified mercury is nectar (Rasaratnākara, Rasa-khaṇḍa 1.30).
summary: A Śaiva tantric science, presented as revealed by Bhairava to the Goddess, that seeks a stable, undecaying 'divine body' through mercury processed with sulphur, mica and other minerals and joined with breath-control, mantra and worship. Its goal is liberation while living (jīvanmukti) in that body; the metal-transmuting work (lohavedha) serves as a test before the body is treated (dehavedha). Its medical side supplied the mercurial and metallic medicines of later Āyurveda. RESTRICTED: recorded here as summary and the texts' own warnings only.
notes: family 'shared': predominantly Śaiva (the Raseśvara is counted among the Māheśvara systems in the Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha), but alchemical works are ascribed to the Buddhist Nāgārjuna and a Jain (Merutuṅga) commented on the Rasādhyāya. No processes, quantities or recipes are recorded anywhere in this unit.
